question: is the per-type/per-field u32 key in the typeinfo/fieldinf tables a digest of the plain identifier string?
verdict: NO.  Every standard / parameterised digest family tested produces zero matches against 2499 VERIFIED (type-name -> typeinfo u32[0]) anchor pairs, and no family beats the noise floor when matched against the full 23701-value universe.

anchor_pairs.source: p2_anchors.json - registration stub -> .data type-info cell -> q0 -> exact typeinfo record base

families: poly(h*M OP c) for 36 multipliers x 19 inits x 4 op-orders
64-bit poly families truncated to low/high 32 bits
schemes_tested_against_anchors.result: 0 hits for every combination (a single hit would have proved the scheme)
schemes_tested_against_anchors.64bit_families_verdict: no family produced a single hit on the 2499 verified (type name -> key) anchors

structural_tests.crc_with_arbitrary_init_pattern: REJECTED - (expected_hash ^ raw_crc32(name)) is not constant inside any name-length group, for any of the 20 record slots
structural_tests.add_family_any_multiplier: REJECTED - for names sharing the last byte every key difference must be divisible by the multiplier; the gcd over 29143 such pairs is 1, so no multiplier > 1 can fit. Same test on the reversed byte order (20808 pairs): gcd 1.
structural_tests.xor_family_any_multiplier: REJECTED - for names sharing the last byte the low 8 bits of the key must match; 29021/29143 pairs violate it (reversed order: 20722/20808).
structural_tests.init_solve_for_candidate_multipliers: for M in {31,33,37,39,41,131,65599,16777619,0x01000193,5381,5,257,65537} and both byte orders, solving the init from one anchor reproduces exactly 1/2499 anchors
structural_tests.scope: these tests are independent of the multiplier and of the initial value, so they exclude the whole class of 32-bit polynomial hashes (and their 64-bit truncations) for the type-name -> key mapping

remaining_unknown: The per-type 32-bit key cannot be reproduced from the type name: it is a build-time id (no code in bf6.exe writes the static records - 0/3590 key-slot stores and 0/3174 kind-slot stores hit a real static record).  What is STILL unknown: the algorithm the Frostbite build tool used, and whether the field keys in the fieldinf section are the same scheme.  What is NOT needed for name resolution: the type names live in .rdata and are referenced by 10172 registration stubs, and the offsets live in the fieldinf payload slots - the names for FIELDS however do not exist anywhere in bf6.exe, they are only materialised in the live process.

key_writer_analysis.question: is there code in bf6.exe that WRITES the per-type u32 key (typeinfo record +0x00)?
key_writer_analysis.method: opcode-valid RIP-relative store refs (forms 6/7/8/15/22/23) from the 4,241,357-ref scan, filtered to targets inside the typeinfo section, then resolved to (record base, offset)
key_writer_analysis.verdict: every one of those stores targets a RUNTIME node (the all-zero regions of the section that the 10172 registration stubs fill) that merely happens to sit inside a static record's 0x50 window - verified by checking that the marker 0x00080089 is NOT present at target+4.  CONCLUSION: no code in the binary writes the static records, so the per-type key is BAKED IN AT BUILD TIME and there is no runtime routine to reverse.

non_registration_store_candidates.details: p2_key_stores.json (function RVA + decoded store instruction + target bytes)

experiment_that_would_crack_it: 1) run the game and read one live typeinfo node: the node stores the type NAME POINTER next to the per-type u32 key -> gives (name, key) pairs that include the runtime-salted variant

2) [RESOLVED - no such routine exists] the per-type key slot is never written by any code in bf6.exe (see key_writer_analysis), so the key is a build-time value; reverse it in the BUILD tooling (Frostbite SDK / fbhash) or in the encrypted reflection blob instead of in the binary
3) reverse the .vlizer / _RDATA sections: one of them likely holds the serialised reflection blob whose pre-image strings are the hash input

fieldinf_candidate_hash_space.method: every u32 of the fieldinf section was classified: 305620 zeros, 147964 'other' values (59366 distinct) of which the bulk are low-32 .data VA halves (type-cell pointers); the remaining large values were matched against 132594 .rdata identifier names hashed with djb2_xor/djb2_add/fnv1a32/mul31/mul131/mul16777619
fieldinf_candidate_hash_space.noise_floor: 117222 distinct hashes x 59366 target values / 2^32 = 1.6 expected hits per family
fieldinf_candidate_hash_space.verdict: all observed hits are at or below the noise floor -> no field-name hash family confirmed

p2_hash_attack.json.question: is the per-type/per-field u32 key in the typeinfo/fieldinf tables a digest of the plain identifier string?
p2_hash_attack.json.verdict: NO.  Every standard / parameterised digest family tested produces zero matches against 2499 VERIFIED (type-name -> typeinfo u32[0]) anchor pairs, and no family beats the noise floor when matched against the full 23701-value universe.
p2_hash_attack.json.remaining_unknown: the exact pre-image string (and therefore the algorithm) behind the u32 keys at typeinfo+0x00 and the field-name key inside fieldinf.  The plain identifier string occurs EXACTLY ONCE in the whole binary (verified for AftermathProcess, ServerAICommanderOrderEntity, ServerActivityEntryComponentInterface) and no qualified/mangled variant exists (0 hits for 'AICommander::ServerAICommanderOrderEntity', 'games::AICommander', 'fb::games', 'fb::' + name).  The keys are therefore computed by a proprietary build-time routine, not by a name digest we can reproduce.
experiment_that_would_crack_it_top: 1) run the game and read one live typeinfo node: the node stores the type NAME POINTER next to the per-type u32 key -> gives (name, key) pairs that include the runtime-salted variant
2) locate the build-time/runtime routine that WRITES typeinfo+0x00 (search .text for stores into the typeinfo section that are not the registration stubs) and read its algorithm
3) reverse the .vlizer / _RDATA sections: one of them likely holds the serialised reflection blob whose pre-image strings are the hash input
